bibliography.abstract: Inter-municipal food networks (IFNs) have become an increasingly prominent vehicle for local governments to develop more social and ecologically sustainable urban food strategies. IFNs are highly diverse, operating at different scales and specializing on different practices, from mutual exchange to policy advocacy, thereby offering a wide range of possibilities for local governments to develop transformative capacities. Yet, surprisingly little research has examined the inter-municipal dynamics and impact of IFNs, as most studies remain focused on individual city case studies. This raises questions about how IFNs operate and to what extent they contribute to sustainable transformations within their member cities. This article explores these questions through a systematic review of academic literature on IFNs. It seeks to identify the scale, governance modes, political activities, as well as drivers and barriers to impact of IFNs studied in the literature. Drawing on the multilevel perspective, the article discusses what we know about IFN's potential for food regime transformation, and which questions remain unanswered. While it finds some indications that IFNs can inspire new urban food strategies and respond to diverse political economic contexts, significant knowledge gaps remain concerning their scale, organizational governance, ambitions and impact, which inhibits a comprehensive assessment of their transformative potential.
bibliography.title: A tale of many cities: The role of inter-municipal food networks in changing the dominant food regime

en.caveats: The analysis is constrained by significant gaps in the existing literature regarding the precise organizational governance, scale, and measurable impacts of these networks, which limits a definitive assessment of their transformative power.
en.what: This study conducts a systematic literature review of academic research on inter-municipal food networks (IFNs) to analyze their scale, governance structures, political activities, and operational barriers. Using a multilevel perspective framework, it synthesizes how these networks of local governments facilitate mutual exchange and policy advocacy to shape urban food strategies.
en.why: It shifts the research focus from isolated, single-city case studies to the collective dynamics of municipal networks, revealing how collaborative local governance can scale up to challenge dominant, unsustainable food regimes.
